summary:
MARSWALK is a browser-based Progressive Web App prototype developed to support interactive exploration and mission planning on Mars. Focused on the boxwork region of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater, it uses NASA's HiRISE imagery as a map background and provides tools for sketching proposed traverses, recording scientific notes, and exporting or importing mission plans. It also features a science panel presenting selected observations from NASA's Curiosity rover mission and a basic 3D visualization of the Martian image.
The project addresses the challenge by bringing planetary imagery, scientific information, exploration-planning tools together in one accessible interface. Users can examine the selected Martian landscape, sketch possible routes using waypoints, document observations in a digital notebook, and share their work through portable mission files. These features demonstrate how different digital tools can support the organization, interpretation of planetary exploration information.
MARSWALK is important because it demonstrates how open NASA data can be transformed into practical educational and exploratory resources. It can help students develop an interest in planetary science, encourage public engagement with space exploration, and provide educators, analogue mission teams with an interactive environment for learning, experimenting with route-planning concepts, and understanding the information that may support future human exploration of Mars.
details:
MARSWALK: Interplanetary Survival Guide – Martian Field Rehearsal Map

1. What does the project do?

MARSWALK is an interactive, offline-capable Progressive Web Application (PWA) designed to make planetary surface exploration and Extra-Vehicular Activity (EVA) decision rehearsal approachable through real NASA and USGS planetary data.

Focusing on the polygonal boxwork ridge sector on the lower slopes of Mount Sharp (Aeolis Mons) in Gale Crater—a key geological target investigated by NASA's Curiosity rover—MARSWALK lets students, educators, and analogue mission planners inspect calibrated Martian imagery, sketch out-and-back traverses, evaluate time budgets, examine rover/orbital evidence, record geolocated field notes, and export portable mission packs.

Instead of treating Mars imagery as a static picture or inventing fake hazard ratings, MARSWALK turns real orbital and rover datasets into an interactive exploration workspace governed by explicit scientific boundaries.

2. How does it work?

MARSWALK integrates several connected tools inside a single browser workspace:

Interactive 2D Martian Map (Leaflet `CRS.Simple`): Displays a calibrated 2048 × 2048 px MRO HiRISE optical crop (PSP_001752_1750_RED, 0.25 m/px, 512 m × 512 m) in bottom-left image-pixel coordinates with pan/zoom, layer toggles, Reset View / Focus Route controls, and full keyboard-accessible point placement.

Route Planner & Out-and-Back Survival Time Budget: Users place, drag, insert, or undo Start, Waypoint, and Destination markers to measure calibrated planar distance (0.25 m/px). An arithmetic Out-and-Back Survival Time Budget combines round-trip distance with user-entered walking speed, science stop duration, safety reserve, and available excursion time—explicitly flagging time deficits without ever claiming terrain safety.

Multi-Source Science Evidence & Provenance Panels: Connects the study site with Curiosity rover observations (Sols 4803, 2121, 236–3251), a side-by-side 2-Record Science Comparison workspace, PDS4 REMS weather excerpts (Sols 3900 & 4803), USGS Geologic Map of Mars (SIM 3292, Hesperian transition unit Htu), Exploration Confidence, Image Passport, and a central Sources, Data & Methods panel. Rover records lack sub-pixel tie-points to the crop and are intentionally kept unpinned (Visual Review Only).

Digital Field Notebook & Guarded Portability: Users attach field notes directly to image coordinates; drafts, routes, brief objectives, and safety declarations persist in localStorage across reloads. Completed plans export as schema- and imageRef-validated .JSON packs or human-readable .TXT Combined Survival Briefs.

Opt-In 3D Terrain Rehearsal (Three.js): Lazy-loads an interactive WebGL viewer supporting both a Pixal3D AI-generated relief mesh (203,522 triangles with tap-to-inspect model angles) and a flat calibrated reference plane—with strict visual isolation so uncalibrated AI geometry never contaminates 2D mission metrics, plus clean GPU disposal on close.

Offline-First PWA Verification: A custom Service Worker downloads, caches, and verifies all 22 runtime assets (9.82 MB) by exact byte length and SHA-256 hash, supporting full offline reload and automatic state recovery when disconnected.

3. What benefits does it have?

Zero-barrier planetary exploration: Runs directly in desktop and mobile browsers without requiring specialized desktop GIS or planetary mapping software.

Science-honest learning: Helps students and educators distinguish verified planetary measurements (calibrated planar scale, raw citations, regional geology) from unavailable telemetry (stereo DEM elevation, slope, trafficability, or life-support limits).

Structured EVA decision practice: Teaches round-trip route planning, time-margin budgeting, and disciplined field observation logging on real Martian terrain.

Offline resilience & portability: Cryptographic offline caching and portable .JSON/.TXT exports allow work to continue offline and transfer cleanly between sessions or teammates.

4. What is the intended impact of the project?

MARSWALK is built to advance accessible planetary literacy and critical scientific reasoning:

For students: Encourages hands-on inquiry in planetary geology, orbital geodesy, EVA constraints, and aerospace software engineering using real mission data.

For educators and science communicators: Replaces passive slide imagery with an interactive lab for exploring Gale Crater's ancient aqueous history and measurement uncertainty.

For analogue EVA teams: Provides a transparent rehearsal scratchpad for planning routes, checking round-trip time margins, and documenting observations before field deployment.

Longer term, MARSWALK provides an extensible open foundation where validated HiRISE stereo Digital Terrain Models (DTMs), multi-site landing zones, and verified surface hazard layers can plug directly into the existing provenance architecture.

5. What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did we use?

Languages & Styling: TypeScript, HTML, SCSS/CSS, Python (geodetic and manifest verification utilities), and JavaScript/Node.js (build and Service Worker tooling).

Frameworks & Libraries: Angular 22 (standalone components and Signals), RxJS, Leaflet (1.9.4) for 2D pixel-space cartography, Three.js (0.187.0) for lazy-loaded WebGL 3D rendering, and self-hosted Inter and Space Grotesk fonts (SIL OFL 1.1).

Storage & Offline Engine: Browser localStorage for resilient mission/draft state, a custom Cache API Service Worker (service-worker.js) with SHA-256 asset verification, and structured .JSON / .TXT mission exports.

Data & Tooling: NASA MRO HiRISE (PSP_001752_1750_RED / PIA26306), NASA Curiosity rover & PDS4 REMS records, USGS SIM 3292 Geologic Map of Mars (GDAL/PyProj/Python), Tencent ARC Pixal3D (used offline to generate the optional illustration GLB), Vitest + JSDOM (308 unit tests), Node test runner (11 PWA tests), Playwright/Chromium, VS Code, Git/GitHub, and Vercel (https://marswalk-spaceapps.vercel.app/).

Hardware: Standard developer laptops/workstations and browser-emulated desktop (1440px), tablet (820px), and smartphone (390px) viewports (with physical mobile home-screen testing identified as next-step validation).

6. How is the project creative?

From static picture to decision simulator: Instead of merely showing a pretty Mars photo or adding gamified sci-fi guesswork, MARSWALK turns a real 512 m × 512 m Mount Sharp boxwork window into an interactive mission-rehearsal instrument.

Honesty as a core UX mechanic: Rather than inventing plausible-looking slope or "safe route" scores, MARSWALK surfaces explicit uncertainty ("Visual Review Only", unavailable DEM/safety fields, unpinned regional rover records, and isolated model-only 3D angles) as an active part of how users plan.

Unified multi-mission synthesis: Combines sub-meter HiRISE optical imagery, Curiosity chemistry/weather records, regional 1:20M USGS geology, out-and-back time budgeting, optional AI 3D relief, and cryptographic offline packaging inside one cohesive, WCAG-accessible workspace.

7. What factors did our team consider?

Scientific relevance: We focused on lower Mount Sharp's boxwork formations in Gale Crater for their aqueous sulfate geological record and ongoing Curiosity investigation.

Data availability and reliability: We audited official NASA (HiRISE, Curiosity, PDS4 REMS) and USGS (SIM 3292) sources, preserving raw metadata, licenses, and provenance manifests.

Geographical context and scale: We paired a calibrated 0.25 m/px HiRISE crop in pixel coordinates with regional 1:20,000,000 USGS stratigraphy (Htu) and refused to invent unverified rover pin coordinates.

Usability and accessibility: We engineered responsive desktop/tablet/phone layouts, full keyboard navigation, WCAG AA high-contrast light and dark themes, and plain-language status indicators.

Data organization and portability: We built resilient localStorage draft retention, schema- and imageRef-guarded .JSON mission import/export, and .TXT Combined Survival Brief exports.

Technical feasibility: We selected a zero-backend Angular + Leaflet + Three.js PWA architecture with SHA-256 offline verification (22 assets) to achieve fast reliability within hackathon constraints.

Scientific limitations and safety honesty: Because verified DEM elevation, slope, obstacle/trafficability data, and life-support modeling are absent—and the Pixal3D 3D relief is uncalibrated illustration—MARSWALK computes calibrated planar distance and arithmetic time budgets only and explicitly refrains from certifying route safety.

Future scalability: Modular panels, declarative manifests, and automated Python/Node verification scripts enable clean integration of stereo HiRISE DTMs and additional Martian study sites.

Project Repository: The complete source code and development files for MARSWALK are available on GitHub: https://github.com/boscopatrick907-coder/NASA_SAPCEAPP_-MARS_WALK-

Conclusion

MARSWALK bridges planetary science, cartography, and accessible web engineering. By uniting calibrated NASA orbital imagery, Curiosity rover/REMS records, USGS regional geology, route and time-budget rehearsal, optional 3D visualization, and explicit scientific boundaries in an offline-capable browser workspace, the project invites users to explore and reason critically about Mars rather than passively view images—establishing a verified, extensible foundation for future planetary education and field planning tools.
